note.text: Quantifiers express quantity: several proposals, much information, a little time. Countability is a property of the noun’s use, so a dictionary and the sentence matter. A few suggests some countable items, while few often emphasises scarcity; a little and little make a similar contrast with an uncountable amount. Qualifiers such as fairly or very can modify the degree of an adjective. They do not automatically provide a numerical measurement. A statement with some or fairly should not be rewritten as all or completely without evidence.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to match quantity expressions to noun uses and explain how a qualifier changes the degree of a description. Builds on: word classes, context and conditional statements. Leads to: resource explanations and appropriately limited claims.

sections.heading: Read the original model
sections.text: Original models: Several members read the fairly clear proposal. A few offered questions, so the number was small but positive. The group needed a little more information. Information is uncountable in this use; an item of information introduces a countable unit. Fairly modifies clear, not the exact attendance.

sections.heading: Apply and check
sections.text: Identify the noun use, then choose a compatible quantifier. For a qualifier, name the word it modifies and the strength of the claim. Preserve small positive quantity, absence and totality as different meanings.

cards.idea: Distinguish the ideas used in this lesson.
example: count quantifier: an expression compatible here with a plural countable noun.

cards.idea: Read the whole example before identifying its function.
example: Several proposals gives a countable quantity.
A little information gives an amount without counting items.
A few attended means some attended.
Fairly qualifies clear in the proposal description.

cards.idea: A correction must preserve the intended meaning and form.
example: Much proposals is the required model. Correction: Much does not fit this plural countable use.
Many information is the ordinary pattern in this use. Correction: Use much or an appropriate amount phrase rather than many.
A few always means no one. Correction: The phrase indicates a small positive number.
Fairly supplies an exact numerical percentage by itself. Correction: A degree word does not automatically supply a measurement.
